questions.question: How do climatologists and environmental economists distinguish between 'weather' and 'climate'?

options.text: Weather refers to permanent shifts in the ozone layer, while climate describes daily atmospheric pressure.

Weather represents short-term atmospheric conditions (temperature, rainfall, humidity) occurring over days or weeks, whereas climate is the statistical average weather pattern observed over decades or longer periods.
Weather applies exclusively to oceanic currents, while climate describes inland soil conditions.
There is no scientific difference; both terms are interchangeable synonyms describing daily rainfall.

questions.explanation: According to Section 8.2.2 of the Grade 12 textbook, weather represents short-term atmospheric conditions expressed through daily or weekly mixes of temperature, precipitation, and humidity. In contrast, climate refers to the average weather conditions and variability over an extended duration, typically decades or longer.
questions.sourceReference: Section 8.2.2, Pages 190-191 & EUEE 2017 EC, Q20, Q50

questions.question: Which anthropogenic greenhouse gas (GhG) is the single largest contributor to global warming and climate change, accounting for approximately 77% of the total greenhouse effect?

options.text: Methane (CH4)
Nitrous oxide (N2O)
Carbon dioxide (CO2)
Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs)

questions.explanation: Section 8.2.3 notes that among the major greenhouse gases generated by human economic activity, carbon dioxide (CO2)—primarily emitted from fossil fuel combustion and deforestation—is the dominant driver of global warming, contributing about 77% to the greenhouse effect, followed by methane at 14% and nitrous oxide at 8%.

questions.question: What is the defining economic characteristic of a 'green economy'?

options.text: An economy that maximizes short-term output by entirely depleting fossil fuels

An economy that improves human wellbeing and social equity while significantly reducing environmental risks and ecological scarcities, characterized by low carbon usage, resource efficiency, and social inclusion
An economy based strictly on the complete nationalization of all rural agricultural farmland
An economy where agricultural output is heavily taxed to subsidize urban heavy industries

questions.explanation: Section 8.3 defines a green economy as one that results in improved human wellbeing and social equity while significantly reducing environmental risks and ecological scarcities. Its core operational features are that it is low-carbon, resource-efficient, and socially inclusive.
questions.sourceReference: Section 8.3, Pages 198-199 & EUEE 2017 EC, Q57 & EUEE 2018 Round 1, Q28

questions.question: Which of the following is an exhaustible, non-renewable source of energy rather than a renewable one?

options.text: Geothermal energy
Solar radiation
Fossil fuels (petroleum, coal, and natural gas)
Hydroelectric power

questions.explanation: Renewable energy sources include solar, wind, geothermal, biomass, and hydropower because they replenish naturally. Fossil fuels (crude oil, natural gas, and coal) are non-renewable, finite mineral assets whose reserves are permanently depleted through extraction and combustion.

questions.question: What strategic policy framework did the Ethiopian government formulate in 2011 to achieve carbon-neutral middle-income status by 2025?

options.text: The Agricultural Quota Enhancement Strategy (AQES)
The Climate Resilient Green Economy (CRGE) Strategy
The State Farm Mechanization Proclamation (SFMP)
The National Industrial Nationalization Protocol (NINP)

questions.explanation: In 2011, Ethiopia formulated the Climate Resilient Green Economy (CRGE) strategy. The CRGE vision aims to build an energy-efficient, carbon-neutral economy that fosters climate resilience while propelling the nation to middle-income status by 2025.
questions.sourceReference: Section 8.4, Pages 199-201 & EUEE 2017 EC, Q29 & EUEE 2018 Round 1, Q29

questions.question: How do environmental economists distinguish between 'mitigation' and 'adaptation' in climate policy?

options.text: Mitigation is undertaken exclusively by private households, while adaptation is exclusively executed by the United Nations.

Mitigation addresses the root causes of climate change by reducing greenhouse gas emissions or enhancing carbon sinks, whereas adaptation addresses the consequences by adjusting human and natural systems to moderate harm from climate changes.
Mitigation deals with coping with flash floods ex-post, while adaptation focuses on banning gasoline-powered motor engines.
There is no difference; both terms describe the calculation of per capita GDP deflators.

questions.explanation: Section 8.2.7 emphasizes that mitigation addresses the causes of climate change (proactive measures to reduce GhG emissions or stabilize atmospheric concentrations, e.g., renewable energy, reforestation). Adaptation is a reactive or coping response addressing the consequences by enabling human and economic systems to adjust to ongoing or expected impacts.
questions.sourceReference: Section 8.2.7, Pages 195-197 & EUEE 2017 EC, Q54, Q56

questions.question: What does the 'Environmental Kuznets Curve' (EKC) hypothesis postulate regarding the relationship between economic growth and environmental degradation?

options.text: Environmental degradation increases linearly and perpetually as per capita income rises.

In the early stages of economic development, pollution and resource degradation increase with rising per capita income, but beyond a critical threshold, further economic growth leads to environmental improvement, forming an inverted-U curve.
High-income industrialized nations invariably generate zero industrial waste.
Developing agrarian economies experience lower rates of soil erosion than high-income financial economies.

questions.explanation: Section 8.1 highlights the Environmental Kuznets Curve hypothesis, which posits an inverted-U relationship: environmental degradation initially intensifies during the early stages of industrialization and growth, but after reaching higher income levels, greater technological efficiency and public willingness to pay for conservation cause pollution to decline.

questions.question: What is the core proposition of the 'poverty-environment nexus' in developing economies?

options.text: Poverty completely insulates rural households from erratic climate hazards.
The poor are simultaneously agents and victims of environmental degradation, as survival pressures force them to deplete marginal natural assets, which in turn deepens their poverty.
Environmental conservation is achievable only by eliminating all rural peasant agriculture.
Economic poverty is caused entirely by international balance of payments surpluses.

questions.explanation: Section 8.1 explores the poverty-environment nexus: poor rural households lack alternative capital or credit and are forced by economic necessity to cultivate fragile hillsides, overgraze pastures, and cut down forests for firewood (acting as agents of degradation). The resulting erosion, water depletion, and declining crop yields immediately destroy their own livelihoods (making them the primary victims).

questions.question: According to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) assessment reviewed in the textbook, why are regions such as Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia considered the most vulnerable to climate change?

options.text: Because they generate over 85% of total worldwide industrial greenhouse gas emissions

Because they are characterized by heavy reliance on climate-sensitive livelihoods (rain-fed agriculture), high poverty incidence, and limited technological and financial adaptive capacity to absorb shocks
Because their populations reside exclusively in high-latitude polar zones
Because they have completely phased out domestic traditional cottage industries

questions.explanation: Vulnerability depends on exposure, sensitivity, and adaptive capacity. Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia face immense exposure to rainfall variability and drying trends, and their economic sensitivity is exceptionally high due to dependency on rain-fed peasant agriculture, while limited financial and infrastructural resources severely constrain their capacity to adapt.

questions.question: In the analysis of autonomous and planned adaptation, which of the following correctly pairs an adaptation mechanism with its operational classification?

options.text: Mobility: avoiding risks across spatial locations (e.g., pastoralist livestock movements or migration)
Storage: eliminating the need for grain reserves during drought
Diversification: concentrating all household labor into a single crop variety
Communal pooling: privatizing municipal water wells for exclusive high-income commercial use

questions.explanation: Section 8.2.7 details the four traditional classes of adaptation strategies: (1) Mobility (distributing risk across space, such as pastoral transhumance), (2) Storage (reducing risk across time through water tanks or grain silos), (3) Diversification (spreading risk across distinct asset and income streams), and (4) Communal pooling (joint resource management and mutual sharing).

questions.question: According to Ethiopia's National Adaptation Programme of Action (NAPA, 2007), which factors are identified as the primary underlying drivers of the country's severe vulnerability to climatic hazards?

options.text: Excessive reliance on nuclear power and thermal coal plants
Heavy dependence on rain-fed subsistence agriculture, low levels of water resource infrastructure development, and rapid population growth
Excessive domestic savings and industrial capacity over-utilization
Complete absence of livestock in lowland agro-ecological zones

questions.explanation: NAPA (2007) identified three fundamental structural factors underpinning Ethiopia's acute vulnerability to droughts and erratic weather: (1) heavy reliance on rain-fed smallholder farming, (2) underdeveloped irrigation and water storage infrastructure, and (3) high population pressure accelerating land degradation.

questions.question: Why do environmental economists emphasize that conventional Gross Domestic Product (GDP) accounting creates a misleading, paradoxical measure of economic wellbeing when environmental resources are depleted?

options.text: Because GDP automatically subtracts the full economic cost of soil erosion and groundwater loss

Because the market liquidation of natural capital (such as clear-cutting forests or extracting minerals) and expenditures to clean up environmental disasters are recorded as positive additions to current GDP, while the permanent depreciation of the nation's natural capital stock is entirely omitted
Because GDP measures only barter trade transactions conducted by rural households
Because national income accounting includes only intangible intellectual services while omitting all physical commodities

questions.explanation: Section 8.1 explains the measurement paradox: unsustainable activities that destroy forests, deplete fisheries, and erode soils appear as positive income/output in current GDP accounts, and cleanup spending following pollution disasters further inflates GDP figures. However, unlike physical capital depreciation, the depletion of natural capital is not deducted, masking the erosion of long-term productive capacity.

questions.question: Under international climate agreements (such as the Kyoto Protocol and Paris Agreement), what is the economic role of market-based mechanisms like the Clean Development Mechanism (CDM) and REDD-plus (Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and Forest Degradation)?

options.text: They mandate that developing nations immediately cease all domestic agricultural production.

They allow industrialized nations to fulfill greenhouse gas reduction commitments by investing in low-cost mitigation and forest conservation projects in developing countries, facilitating technology transfer and carbon-finance inflows to low-income nations.
They prohibit private international carbon-offset trading across sovereign borders.
They establish universal uniform import tariffs on solar panels and wind turbines.

questions.explanation: Section 8.2.7 details that mechanisms such as the CDM and REDD-plus create economic incentives for carbon reduction by allowing high-abatement-cost industrialized nations to fund emission reduction, reforestation, and forest conservation projects in developing economies. This achieves global cost-effectiveness while providing developing nations with clean technologies and financial resources.

questions.question: What are the four core programmatic pillars of Ethiopia's Climate Resilient Green Economy (CRGE) strategy designed to achieve sustainable economic transformation?

options.text: Promoting fossil-fuel thermal plants, expanding pastoral land clearing, subsidizing diesel trucks, and privatizing municipal water sources

Improving crop and livestock production practices for higher food security; protecting and re-establishing forests for economic and ecosystem services; expanding electricity generation from renewable energy (hydro, wind, geothermal); and leapfrogging to modern, energy-efficient technologies in transport, industry, and buildings
Nationalizing commercial bank foreign reserves, banning domestic fertilizer manufacturing, and imposing mandatory grain delivery quotas
Devaluing the currency by 300% and eliminating all rural public schools and clinics

questions.explanation: Section 8.4 outlines the four central pillars of the CRGE initiative: (1) adopting advanced agricultural and livestock practices to boost food yields without expanding emissions, (2) protecting and expanding forests (including the Green Legacy Initiative), (3) harnessing abundant renewable energy (hydropower, geothermal, wind, solar), and (4) deploying energy-efficient technologies in transport and industrial production.
questions.sourceReference: Section 8.4, Pages 199-201 & EUEE 2017 EC, Q29 & EUEE 2018 Round 1, Q27

questions.question: In the analysis of rural development and the environment, how do population pressure and agricultural 'extensification' compare with 'intensification' regarding their specific environmental impacts in the Ethiopian highlands?

options.text: Extensification uses heavy chemical pesticides on small plots, while intensification causes rural-to-urban outmigration.

Extensification involves clearing marginal lands, steep hillsides, and forests to expand crop area, causing deforestation and biodiversity loss; intensification involves continuous farming on existing plots without adequate fallow, leading to nutrient depletion, soil structure loss, and potential chemical runoff from inorganic fertilizers.
Both processes eliminate soil erosion and guarantee permanent environmental restoration.
Extensification is strictly confined to urban industrial zones, while intensification occurs only in lowland pastoral ranges.

questions.explanation: Section 8.1.1 examines the twin pressures of extensification (expanding agricultural area by clearing forests and encroaching on fragile marginal slopes, driving deforestation and accelerated water erosion) and intensification (farming shrinking fragmented plots more frequently without fallow periods or conservation inputs, which depletes organic matter, destroys soil water-holding capacity, and risks soil salinization/chemical degradation).
questions.sourceReference: Section 8.1.1, Pages 185-186 & EUEE 2017 EC, Q18, Q19
